ai.literal: Desire, they say, for all living beings, at all times, is the seed that yields unceasing birth.
ai.translation: Desire, they say, is the seed that yields an endless cycle of births for all living beings at all times.
ai.modern: எல்லா உயிர்களுக்கும் எக்காலத்திலும் அழியாத பிறவித்துன்பத்தைத் தரும் விதை ஆசை என்று கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the root cause of the cycle of rebirths. The author identifies 'அவா' (desire) as the primary seed ('வித்து') that continuously generates new births ('பிறப்பு') for all living beings. The word 'தவாஅ' is an elongated form meaning 'unceasing' or 'never-ending', emphasizing that as long as desire exists, the cycle of birth and death will never stop. By calling desire the 'seed', the couplet highlights that just as a seed inevitably grows into a plant, desire inevitably manifests as future existence.

ai.literal: When desiring, one should desire non-birth; and that, by desiring desirelessness, will come.
ai.translation: If one must desire anything, let it be the state of not being born again; and that state of non-birth will be attained by desiring desirelessness.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் எதையாவது விரும்ப வேண்டும் என்றால், அவர் மீண்டும் பிறக்காமல் இருக்கும் நிலையையே விரும்ப வேண்டும்; அந்தப் பிறவாமை என்னும் நிலை, ஆசையற்ற தன்மையை (வேண்டாமையை) விரும்புவதால் மட்டுமே உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that if a person wishes to desire anything at all, the ultimate and only worthy goal is to desire 'non-birth'—the freedom from the cycle of rebirths. The author then reveals how this supreme state is attained: it comes simply by desiring 'desirelessness' itself. By redirecting all our desires toward wanting nothing, we cut off the root cause of rebirth. The clever repetition of the root word 'வேண்டு' (to desire) emphasizes that the path to absolute freedom lies in mastering and redirecting our own desires.

ai.literal: Desirelessness like supreme wealth here is not; there also that equal is not.
ai.translation: There is no supreme wealth in this world like desirelessness; even in the other world, there is nothing equal to it.
ai.modern: ஆசையின்மை போன்ற சிறந்த செல்வம் இவ்வுலகில் இல்லை; அவ்வுலகிலும் அதற்கு இணையானது எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of desirelessness (வேண்டாமை), describing it as the greatest possible wealth. The author asserts that in this earthly life (ஈண்டு), there is no treasure that compares to being free from desires. Furthermore, even in the other world or any higher state of existence (ஆண்டு), there is absolutely nothing that can equal the profound peace and richness of having no wants.

ai.literal: Purity is that which is called desire's absence; and that, truthfulness if desired, will come.
ai.translation: Purity is said to be the absence of desire; and that state will come to those who desire the ultimate truth.
ai.modern: தூய்மை என்பது ஆசைகள் இல்லாமல் இருப்பது ஆகும்; அந்த ஆசையற்ற நிலை மெய்ம்மையை விரும்பினால் உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true purity not as physical cleanliness, but as the complete absence of desire. It then explains how this state of desirelessness can be achieved: it comes naturally when one desires and seeks the ultimate truth. By shifting one's focus from transient worldly desires to the eternal truth, all other limiting desires fade away. The poet uses phonetic elongation in the words for purity and truth to emphasize their supreme importance.

ai.literal: Those who are detached, they say, are those who are free from desire; others, in that manner, do not have detachment.
ai.translation: Those who are truly detached are those who have freed themselves from desire; all others, though they may have renounced other things, are not truly detached.
ai.modern: பற்றுகளை அறுத்தவர் என்று சொல்லப்படுபவர் ஆசைகளை அறுத்தவரே ஆவர்; மற்றவர்கள் வேறு எவற்றைத் துறந்திருந்தாலும், முழுமையாகத் துறந்தவர்கள் ஆக மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate nature of true renunciation. The poet states that only those who have completely eradicated desire (அவா) can be called truly detached (அற்றவர்). Others (மற்றையார்) might have given up their wealth, family, or worldly possessions, but if they still harbor desire in their minds, they have not achieved complete detachment (அற்றது இலர்). The core message is that desire is the root of all attachment, and renouncing everything else is meaningless if desire itself remains.

ai.literal: Fearing [what is to be feared], indeed, is virtue; that which deceives a person, indeed, is desire.
ai.translation: Fearing what ought to be feared is indeed virtue; that which utterly deceives a person is desire.
ai.modern: அஞ்ச வேண்டிய தீமைகளுக்கு அஞ்சுவதே ஒருவருக்கு அறமாகும்; ஒருவனை ஏமாற்றி அழிப்பது பேராசையே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the protective nature of healthy fear with the destructive nature of desire. The poet states that fearing things that should be feared, such as vice or moral transgression, is actually a form of virtue because it keeps a person on the right path. In contrast, desire is identified as the ultimate deceiver, which secretly misleads a person and brings about their ruin. By using the particle 'ōrum' (meaning 'if one considers' or 'surely') with both concepts, the couplet invites deep reflection on what truly protects us versus what secretly betrays us.

ai.literal: If one cuts off desire completely, the unfailing state will come in the very manner oneself wishes.
ai.translation: If a person completely cuts off desire, the eternal, unfailing state of liberation will come to them in the very way they wish.
ai.modern: ஆசையை முழுமையாக ஒழித்துவிட்டால், அழியாத பேரின்ப நிலை தான் விரும்பும் வழியிலேயே வந்து சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the ultimate reward of conquering desire. The word 'அவாவினை' refers to desire, which binds the soul, and 'ஆற்ற அறுப்பின்' means to sever it completely. When desire is totally eliminated, 'தவாவினை'—the unfailing, eternal state of liberation or supreme peace—comes naturally. The phrase 'தான்வேண்டு மாற்றான்' (தான் வேண்டும் ஆற்றான்) indicates that this ultimate state will manifest in the exact manner that the seeker wishes, showing that true freedom brings absolute mastery over one's destiny.

ai.literal: To those who do not have desire, suffering will not exist; if that exists, it will come without ceasing, more and more.
ai.translation: For those who are free from desire, there is no suffering; but if desire exists, suffering will come upon them endlessly, more and more.
ai.modern: ஆசை இல்லாதவர்களுக்குத் துன்பம் இல்லை; அந்த ஆசை இருக்குமானால், துன்பம் குறையாமல் மேலும் மேலும் வந்து சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the direct relationship between desire and suffering. For those who have completely eliminated desire (அவா), there is no sorrow in life. However, if desire is allowed to exist (அஃதுண்டேல்), suffering will continuously and endlessly (தவாஅது) multiply and come upon them (மேன்மேல் வரும்). The word 'தவாஅது' is a poetic form (alapeṭai) of 'தவாது', meaning 'without decreasing' or 'ceaselessly', emphasizing the relentless nature of desire-induced pain.

ai.literal: Happiness without interruption will accumulate, desire which is called among sufferings the suffering if destroyed.
ai.translation: If desire, which is the greatest suffering of all sufferings, is destroyed, uninterrupted happiness will crowd in.
ai.modern: துன்பங்கள் எல்லாவற்றிலும் பெரும் துன்பம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஆசை அழிந்துவிட்டால், இடைவிடாத இன்பம் வந்து பெருகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that desire is not just one of many problems, but the ultimate source of misery, described here as the 'suffering of sufferings' (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம்). When this root cause of pain is completely eliminated, true happiness (இன்பம்) naturally rushes in without any gap or interruption (இடையறாது). The word 'ஈண்டும்' beautifully suggests that joy will crowd in and fill the space once occupied by craving. Thus, the eradication of desire is presented as the single key to experiencing continuous, everlasting peace.

ai.literal: If one renounces desire of an insatiable nature, that very state an unshakable nature will give.
ai.translation: If one renounces desire, whose nature is never to be satisfied, that very moment will yield the changeless state of eternal freedom.
ai.modern: நிறைவடையாத இயல்புடைய ஆசையை ஒருவன் நீக்கினால், அந்த நிலையே அவனுக்கு என்றும் அழியாத நிலைத்த தன்மையைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts two kinds of 'iyarkai' (nature or state): the insatiable nature of desire and the changeless nature of liberation. Desire is described as 'ārā iyarkai' because it can never be filled or satisfied; the more it is fed, the more it grows. If a person completely relinquishes this endless desire, they immediately enter 'annilaiyē' (that very state). This shift bestows 'pērā iyarkai', a permanent, unwavering state of peace that never departs.
